content.comment_body: Hello everyone. I've bought a SCT-013-000 100A non-invasive current sensor to use on the mains grid side of my electricity supply. The sensor outputs 0-50mA analog current, which I need to convert to match the 0-20mA or 0-10V analog input of my [product_name] ([article_no]). This device controls valves for a micro hydro setup, and the sensor will monitor exported power. Any suggestions on the most effective way to do this are welcome. Thank you.

Do you have a datasheet for this sensor? You didn't mention the manufacturer, and searching online shows different specs for the SCT-013-000. If the output is 0-50mA, you could use a 200Ω resistor to get 10V (200Ω * 0.05A = 10V).

Thanks for replying. Here’s the datasheet and the manufacturer is YHDC. What's confusing is there’s no reference to a supply voltage. I have another DC sensor on the inverter that uses a 5VDC supply and outputs 0-2.5V—it works fine—but the SCT-013-000 datasheet doesn't specify this. [url] Thanks again.
It looks like the sensor outputs AC rather than DC.

Hello [user_name], this sensor won’t work directly with the [product_name] without some type of converter circuit. It's more suited to Arduino, Raspberry Pi, or ESP platforms. Ideally, you should get a sensor specifically designed for the [product_name]. For example, look at the AT-100 B10 or AT-B420L from the LEM AT-B series. Greetings [user_name] (translated with Google)

Greetings [user_name], I understand, thank you. The LEM sensors seem expensive, around £100. I found a split-core sensor online that’s much more affordable: [url] I can't disturb the cables, so the split-core design is necessary, and a 100A rating offers more flexibility than 50A for a household supply. The CS-SP10 version looks suitable. Do you think this would work? Thanks again, [user_name]
Why do you think so? Do you have experience using Arduino, Raspberry Pi, or ESP? If yes, please share more details.

Yes, that option seems promising and reasonably priced. Plus, you get a direct connection to the [product_name] without any DIY intermediate steps. What’s missing is info about dielectric strength (AC/DC) and basic insulation as per IEC 61010-1, along with overvoltage category CAT III and other details. Also, the diagram starts at 1V, which is a bit confusing. With a tolerance of 1%, you need to decide if the accuracy suits your needs. The sensor should work with the [product_name], but keep in mind it only resolves up to a value of 1000, meaning steps of 100mA. Generally, higher-quality and more accurate sensors do cost more—sometimes even more than the controller itself. I've installed sensors costing five figures before. Greetings [user_name]
Thanks for the advice. After some searching on Ebay, I found a new surplus LEM Current Sensor AT 50 B10 at a much lower price. I only need to measure up to around 12kW.
You wrote that, not me. Please explain why you think so...

Thanks again for all the advice. I’ve now installed the LEM AT 50 B10. It gives reliable readings to the [product_name], but the readings are positive regardless of current flow direction. Is there a method to determine if energy is being imported or exported? There's an arrow on the sensor for installation (set towards the grid to measure export), but the [product_name] always shows a positive voltage no matter the flow. Thank you.

Good choice! The sensor outputs a voltage based on current flow, regardless of direction. You initially mentioned supplying power to the grid, not drawing it. You may need to check if you can sense the difference when power generation is active. Greetings [user_name] (translated with Google)

Thanks for your response. It’s a small property with single-phase grid connection, plus a micro-hydro generator that provides power to different areas. The current flow at the CT sensor changes unexpectedly between importing and exporting, based on local load and generated power (from 0–6kW). The 0–10V CT sensor gives an AC current value, but not the direction, which makes the data hard to use. One workaround is installing three matching CT sensors and calculating the values: S1: CT on generator output (generated power), S2: CT on house supply (power consumed by house), S3: CT on other parts (generated power minus rest consumed). Example: S1-(S1-(S1-S3)+S2. Positive values mean export, negative mean import. But extra sensors and additional [product_name] modules for more analog inputs add cost and complexity, when all I really need is to know which direction the AC power flows at the grid connection. Ideally, I want a flow direction sensor that reverses the CT’s 0-10V output depending on whether power is imported or exported. Any advice is welcome – thanks!

analysis.insight_summary: Users are trying to connect a third-party current sensor to a [product_name] to monitor export power in a micro-hydro system. The challenge is converting the sensor’s output to match the analog input requirements of the [product_name]. There are questions about sensor specifications, signal type, and supply voltage, as well as concerns about the high cost and compatibility of suitable sensors. Issues around measurement precision, standards compliance, and data resolution are discussed, highlighting the difficulties of integrating third-party sensors with [product_name] controllers.
analysis.user_expectations: Users expect to easily adapt a third-party current sensor’s output to [product_name] analog inputs for reliable and accurate current measurement, without needing expensive or complicated additional hardware.
